query: For titanium alloys used as structural materials, formulate one hypothesis for an intervention that could increase surface hardness and wear resistance. Specify the intervention, its proposed mechanism, the expected improvement relative to the untreated alloy, the service or test conditions under which the effect should hold, prior evidence supporting the hypothesis, and a controlled experiment with clear results that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a high‐temperature diffusion carburizing treatment to a titanium alloy (e.g. Ti–6Al–4V) will form a thin, continuous TiC surface layer that significantly increases the surface hardness and wear resistance.
generation.material_initial_state: Untreated Ti–6Al–4V alloy exhibiting a typical microstructure and moderate surface hardness (e.g. ~300–400 HV) with relatively higher wear rates under dry sliding conditions.
generation.intervention: Expose the titanium alloy to a controlled carbon-rich atmosphere at elevated temperatures (diffusion carburizing) to promote in situ formation of TiC at the surface.
generation.conditions: The effect is expected under ambient (room temperature) dry sliding wear conditions – for example, in a ball‐on‐disk test at a load of about 10 N and a sliding velocity of approximately 500 mm/s – and can be further evaluated under typical structural service environments.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a continuous layer of fine TiC particles (or a nanostructured TiC phase) on the alloy surface, which acts as a hard, wear‐resistant barrier.
generation.mechanism: During carburizing, carbon diffuses into the titanium substrate, reacting with titanium to form chemically bonded TiC. This TiC layer provides dispersion strengthening and a barrier against plastic deformation, thereby increasing surface hardness and reducing material loss during wear.
generation.predicted_outcome: The treated alloy will exhibit an approximate 30–40% increase in surface hardness and about a 50% reduction in wear rate relative to the untreated alloy.
generation.baseline: Untreated Ti–6Al–4V with a measured hardness around 300–400 HV and a higher wear rate as determined by a standard ball‐on‐disk wear test.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effect is contingent on achieving an optimal diffusion depth and uniform TiC layer; excessive or uneven carbide formation could induce brittleness. Improvements may also vary with differences in process parameters (temperature, time, carbon activity) and testing conditions (load, sliding speed, environment).
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative improvements depend on precise carburizing parameters and may vary with sample preparation. Moreover, potential trade-offs between surface hardness and toughness (brittleness) remain to be fully quantified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical Ti–6Al–4V samples. Subject one set to a controlled high‐temperature diffusion carburizing treatment designed to form a surface TiC layer, while retaining an untreated control set. After processing, run both sets under identical ball‐on‐disk wear tests (e.g., 10 N load, 500 mm/s sliding speed) and measure surface microhardness.
measurements: Wear rate (mm³/N·m) via standardized ball‐on‐disk tests
Microstructural characterization (SEM/EDS/XRD) to confirm TiC phase formation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the carburized samples do not show a statistically significant increase in surface hardness (at least 30% higher than control) or a corresponding decrease in wear rate (at least 30–50% lower) relative to the untreated samples, or if microstructural analysis fails to confirm the formation of a continuous TiC layer, then the hypothesis is falsified.

AbstractThe working environment of agricultural knives is bad, which makes the knives wear out easily. A wear resistant layer of AlCoCrFeNi high entropy alloy (HEA) reinforced by tungsten carbide (WC) was prepared by laser cladding on one side of the cutting edge of a 65 Mn silage knife. Both the effects of WC addition on the microstructure and mechanical properties of AlCoCrFeNi (WC)x (x = 0, 0.1, 0.2 and 0.3 in mass percentage) alloys were investigated. All experimental alloys displayed a crystalline structure of simple body centered cubic (BCC). The hardness of the cladding layer increases with the increase of WC content, and the hardness value enhances from 740 HV0.2 to 1060 HV0.2. A self-grinding edge was formed during working for the cladded knives. The cutting quality can be improved and the service life of agricultural knives can be increased meanwhile. The weight loss rate of untreated knives was about 2.64 times that of the cladded knives after a 76 h field experiment.Keywords: high entropy alloy, WC particles, self-grinding, microstructure, wear resistance
